name: Macedonian combined arms (Philip II and Alexander)

weightNotes.aggression: Alexander attacked at once at the Granicus, sought out Darius at Issus and Gaugamela and pursued him across Iran; offensive at every level.
weightNotes.maneuver: Oblique advance to the right at Gaugamela to pull Persian cavalry out of line; the night crossing of the monsoon-swollen Hydaspes to take Porus in the flank. Manoeuvre-leaning but still fought set-piece battles.
weightNotes.flanking: The Companion cavalry, in wedge formation, was the hammer that struck into a gap or flank while the phalanx held (Companion cavalry article; Gaugamela).
weightNotes.siegePreference: Took every Persian naval base before marching inland (Tyre 332 by mole and ship-borne engines, Gaza), yet the aim was always the decisive field battle with the king. Balanced.
weightNotes.reserveUse: At Gaugamela a second line was posted to face about against envelopment; otherwise most of the army was committed. Moderate-low.
weightNotes.scouting: Prodromoi light cavalry screened and scouted; Engels shows campaigns planned on intelligence about harvests, water and routes. Above mid.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Basis: share of starting strength lost (killed, wounded, captured, missing) at the moment of withdrawal or break, never the battle total with pursuit. derived:breakpoint-quartile: modelRules.breakpoint.loserCasualtyShareAtBreak.iron mid 0.14, grade C. Cohesion of the phalangites and Companions belongs in snapshot cohesion; no non-backtest battle gives a share at withdrawal (Alexander's army never withdrew in a pitched battle). Era baseline.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Sarissa phalanx, hypaspists, Companion and Thessalian heavy cavalry, light cavalry, Agrianian javelinmen, Cretan archers and a siege train used together in one plan. The ancient benchmark.
weightNotes.initiative: Parmenion commanded the left independently and detachments (Craterus at the Hydaspes) acted on their own; but the decisive blow depended on Alexander leading it in person.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Engels (Alexander and the Logistics of the Macedonian Army): Philip cut the baggage train and carts, soldiers carried their own kit, routes were timed to harvests and fleet supply. The Gedrosian march (325) is the exception that proves the cost.

summary: Philip II built a professional army around a deep phalanx of pikemen with the 5-6 m sarissa, which fixed the enemy line frontally (the anvil), while heavy shock cavalry led by the king (the Companions) struck the decisive blow into a flank or a gap (the hammer). Light infantry, archers and Thessalian cavalry covered the joints and the other wing. A lean baggage train and a siege corps let it march fast and take fortified cities. Alexander added operational daring: rapid pursuits, river crossings and sieges of island cities.
whyItWorked: Each arm covered the others' weakness: the phalanx pinned the enemy and held the defensive wing, the cavalry exploited the moment, light troops protected the flanks. Professional drill and Engels-style logistics gave speed and staying power; siege capability meant no fortress could stop a campaign.
whereItFailed: The system depended on the cavalry and the king: without them the phalanx alone was brittle on rough ground and against flexible infantry. Cynoscephalae (197) and Pydna (168): Roman maniples exploited gaps when the phalanx lost cohesion on uneven ground and attacked its exposed flanks. Under Alexander, logistics overreach in the Gedrosian desert (325) cost heavy losses outside battle.

sources.title: Engels, Alexander the Great and the Logistics of the Macedonian Army (1978)
